slides.title: The tank is lower today
slides.text: The camp's water tank held 80 liters yesterday. Today the gauge reads 60. Tally wants one number that says how big the drop is, whatever the size of the tank.

slides.title: Percent change: compare with the start
slides.text: A percent change compares the change with the starting amount. The tank dropped 20 liters from 80, and 20 ÷ 80 = 0.25, so it dropped 25%. Always divide by where you started, not by where you ended.

visual.label: A tank of 80 liters with 20 liters gone

focus.cue: The start: the whole tank, 80 liters.
The change: 20 of the 80 liters, which is 25%.

slides.title: A percent increase
slides.text: A field gave 40 sacks of grain last year and 52 this year. Find the change first, then divide by the starting amount. Check it: 30% of 40 is 12, and 40 + 12 = 52.

slides.title: Percent error
slides.text: Percent error says how far off a measurement is, compared with the real value. A survey says 48 meters where the real distance is 50. It is 2 meters off, and 2 ÷ 50 = 0.04, so the percent error is 4%.

visual.label: Meters off and percent error for a real distance of 50 meters

focus.cue: Each meter off is 1 ÷ 50, which is 2%.

slides.title: Before and after
slides.text: To find an amount after a 15% increase, add 15% of the start: a 200 meter path becomes 200 + 30 = 230 meters. Working backward is different. If a tank holds 40 liters after a 20% drop, then 40 liters is 80% of the start. Each 1% is 40 ÷ 80 = 0.5 liters, so the start was 50 liters.

words.means: the change as a percent of the starting amount
how much an amount grew, as a percent of where it started
how much an amount fell, as a percent of where it started
how far off a measurement is, as a percent of the real value

slides.title: Your mission
slides.text: Open Scale Scout at Percent Report. Set the percent a tank dropped and a field grew, find a survey's percent error, and work out amounts before and after a change. Run each plan to test it.
slides.alt: Scale Scout on a phone: a bar for a water tank of 80 liters filled to 60, with a stepper to set the percent it dropped.
